content: When taking rifapentine or a rifampicin-based tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), it is recommended to use an alternative or barrier form of contraception, as these medications can interfere with the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Parents or legal guardians should be aware that providing TPT to their children can protect them from developing tuberculosis (TB), a disease that is often difficult to diagnose and can have long-term negative health consequences. Child-friendly medications that dissolve in water and have a pleasant taste are now available, making it easier for children to adhere to their treatment regimen. Tuberculosis is a contagious disease transmitted through the air when an individual with active TB coughs. Even with treatment, TB is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Furthermore, individuals who successfully complete TB treatment may still experience lasting damage to their lungs or other organs, which can severely impact their quality of life. However, TB is preventable, and prevention is far more effective than cure. Strategies to prevent TB include early detection and treatment of active TB cases, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination for infants, and providing TPT to individuals who are at high risk of developing TB or have been exposed to the disease. Countries have committed to reducing the number of new TB cases by providing TPT to individuals who have been exposed to TB or are at risk of developing the disease, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV) and family members of TB patients. Administering TPT to these groups can prevent the progression to active TB disease and contribute to a healthier community. TB infection is highly prevalent, but individuals receiving TPT are not sick, do not exhibit symptoms, and are not contagious. TPT is prescribed to reduce the future risk of developing active TB disease, thereby protecting both the individual and the community. The medications used for TPT are generally safe, and shorter TPT regimens combining isoniazid with rifapentine or rifampicin are now available. These regimens are effective in preventing TB progression, have fewer side effects, and are easier to complete. Despite the benefits, it can be challenging for asymptomatic individuals with TB infection to understand the need for preventive treatment. Shorter TPT regimens, which can be completed in 4 to 12 weeks, are now available and must be completed as prescribed to be effective. Support systems involving community health workers, TB survivors, civil society organizations, and non-governmental organizations can help individuals adhere to and complete their TPT. Preventing TB in adults also protects children from exposure to the disease, allowing them to grow up healthier. Similarly, keeping PLHIV free from TB reduces their suffering and helps them live longer, healthier lives. PLHIV who are responding well to antiretroviral therapy (ART) may still acquire TB, and their infection may go unnoticed until it is too late. Taking TPT ensures protection against TB disease, and not taking it represents a missed opportunity to prevent unnecessary illness or death. Most children who contract TB are infected by an adult, often a household member. These children are at higher risk of developing TB in subsequent years and would benefit from TPT. When a family member is diagnosed with TB, it is crucial to evaluate and encourage other family members, including children, to take TPT. There is a need to raise awareness and generate demand for TPT within communities. Sharing accurate information and promoting TPT among at-risk populations can improve its uptake. Advocacy efforts by PLHIV communities, TB survivors, and civil society organizations are essential for symptom screening, encouraging access to TPT, and lobbying for resource allocation to expand TPT availability. TB is one of the top 10 causes of death globally and is caused by bacteria transmitted through the air. If TB bacteria enter the body, they may either be killed by the immune system or remain dormant, potentially becoming active later if the immune system weakens. Conditions such as HIV infection, diabetes, and silicosis, as well as certain medications, can lower immunity and increase the risk of TB progression. Treating TB infection, even in the absence of symptoms, is crucial to prevent the disease from becoming active. Testing for TB infection can be done using the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), though these tests are not required for initiating TPT in PLHIV or child household contacts under five years of age. Target groups for TPT include PLHIV, close contacts of TB patients, and individuals with clinical risk factors such as those undergoing dialysis or preparing for organ transplantation. Several TPT regimens are available, including once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 12 weeks (3HP), daily isoniazid plus rifapentine for one month (1HP), and daily rifampicin plus isoniazid for three months (3HR). These regimens are effective, well-tolerated, and suitable for various populations, including PLHIV and children. Vitamin B6 supplementation may be recommended for individuals on isoniazid-containing regimens to prevent peripheral neuropathy. Pregnant women living with HIV are at risk for TB, which can have severe consequences for both the mother and the unborn child. Pregnancy should not disqualify women from receiving TPT, though close monitoring for side effects is necessary. Taking TPT is essential for individuals at increased risk of developing active TB disease, even if they do not feel ill. Completing the full course of TPT can prevent the infection from progressing to active disease. If adverse drug reactions occur, individuals should contact their healthcare provider immediately. To achieve global TB prevention goals, countries, partners, donors, and communities must work together to integrate TPT into comprehensive TB elimination strategies, strengthen contact investigations, expand TPT in HIV services, and ensure adherence to and completion of TPT regimens. Overcoming barriers to TPT scale-up requires collective efforts and investment to protect individuals and communities from TB.
